questions.prompt: Why does a common-gate stage usually have a much wider bandwidth than a CS stage with the same gain?
options: Its gate is AC ground, so no capacitor connects input to output and nothing is Miller-multiplied
Because its output resistance is smaller
questions.explanation: \(C_{gs}\) loads the low-impedance source node and \(C_{gd}\) loads the output to ground (reader Sec. 14.9).

questions.prompt: A CG stage is driven from \(R_s = 1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and has \(g_m = 4\ \mathrm{mS}\) and \(C_{gs} = 40\ \mathrm{fF}\) at the source node. Find the input pole in GHz.
questions.explanation: The source node sees \(R_s\parallel1/g_m = 1\ \mathrm{k}\parallel250 = 200\ \Omega\), so \(f = 1/(2\pi\cdot200\cdot40\ \mathrm{fF}) = 19.9\ \mathrm{GHz}\). Using \(R_s\) alone gives 4 GHz.

questions.prompt: In a typical CG stage, which pole dominates?
options: The input pole, because \(C_{gs}\) is the largest capacitance
The output pole, because the drain node has the large resistance
A Miller pole at the gate
questions.explanation: The source node's resistance is at most \(1/g_m\), while the drain sees \(R_L\).

questions.prompt: Combine both poles: \(R_s = 1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(g_m = 4\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(C_{gs} = 40\ \mathrm{fF}\), \(R_L = 10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(C_{out} = 50\ \mathrm{fF}\) (\(r_o\) ignored). Find the \(-3\ \mathrm{dB}\) frequency in MHz.
questions.explanation: The poles are at 19.9 GHz and 318 MHz, so the output pole sets the bandwidth almost alone: about 318 MHz. Without a bridging capacitor the two poles do not interact.
questions.figure_alt: Bode magnitude of the CG stage: flat midband, a dominant output pole in the hundreds of megahertz and a far input pole near 20 GHz.

questions.prompt: A CS stage and a CG stage have the same gain and the same \(R_s\). Which usually has the lower bandwidth and why?
options: The CG stage, because its gate is grounded
The CS stage, because its \(C_{gd}\) appears multiplied by the gain at the high-resistance input
questions.explanation: Miller multiplication is the CS stage's penalty; the CG stage pays only for \(C_{gs}\) at a low-resistance node.

questions.prompt: With a finite \(r_o\), why does the CG analysis become less clean?
options: The input resistance then depends on the load, so the input and output nodes interact
questions.explanation: \(R_{in} = (r_o + R_L)/(1 + g_mr_o)\) couples the two nodes; the single-pole picture is then an approximation.
